title: What are foundation models?
text:
What are foundation models?
Conventionally, if you want a model 
to do task T, you have to… 
1. collect lots of labeled data for T 
(e.g., supervised learning) 
2. design a suitable architecture 
3. initialize it randomly 
4. train and validate
3
This shift happened largely 
over the past 4-8 years.
But now…

title: What might we want from foundation models?
text:
What might we want from foundation models?
1.
Language: Understand our requests. 
2.
Knowledge: Know enough about the world to be useful. 
3.
Alignment: Actually follow our instructions. 
4.
Capability: Be effective at following them. 
5.
Safety: But don’t do destructive things, even if asked. 
6.
In-Context Learning: Learn new skills quickly from examples. 
7.
Reasoning: Think longer, consider alternatives, and correct itself if needed. 
8.
Retrieval and Tool Use: Search for information if it’s not sure. 
9.
…
4
How?

title: Deep Learning: Data is the most important element
text:
Deep Learning: Data is the most important element
• One perspective: We aren’t very good at designing detailed 
inductive biases for our world and languages. 
• Design them by data! This is extremely iterative and heuristic. 
• People used to filter out any snippets on the Web that looked 
like they contained code (e.g., curly braces “{“). 
• Now, you pay special attention to having lots of good code!
5

title: Self-Supervised Learning: What can language modeling on Web text do?
text:
Self-Supervised Learning: What can language modeling on Web text do?
• The Eiffel Tower is located in ________, France. [factual knowledge] 
• She crossed the street, checking for traffic over ___ shoulder. [syntax & coreference] 
• The value I got from the two hours watching this movie was the sum total of the 
popcorn and the drink. The movie was ___. [sentiment] 
• A shirt is $40 but we have a 25% discount; the sale price is $___. [math word problems] 
• You are Albert Einstein. You solved this tricky physics problem… [prompting!!] 
• def solve(problem): _________ [code generation] 
An early bet: The only way an LLM can reliably predict the next token at scale is if it 
can model the complexity of the phenomenon the text revolves around! (??)
6
Slightly modified examples from John Hewitt and Chris Manning.

title: “Train on the Web”
text:
“Train on the Web”
• Must crawl pages, starting from seed links! 
• The average page is useless gibberish. How to handle this? 
• Idea #1: Over-sample certain sites! Wikipedia, arXiv, GitHub? 
• Idea #2: Filter based on known heuristics! Upvotes? PageRank? 
• Idea #3: Ask an LLM to “assess quality” and distill into a tiny model. 
• Pages that remain still need a ton of cleaning and deduplication… 
HTML, JavaScript, Boilerplate → clean text for next token prediction.

title: ML is in a deep evals crisis…
text:
ML is in a deep evals crisis… 
Contamination. How do you ensure benchmarks are not in your pre-training data? 
Explicit hill-climbing. By ‘23, LLMs switched from “few-shot learners” to 
aggressive training & validation on all benchmarks. (Sometimes test sets, too! Hopefully at least transparently!) 
Emergence. Capabilities “emerge” from lots of data. This often makes it easier to 
build a system for task T than to reliably evaluate capability T!
Let’s Verify Step by Step (2023)

title: Idea #1: Train M models on equal compute each. Pick best!
text:
Idea #1: Train M models on equal compute each. Pick best!
• e.g., Train 30 models and pick best on validation! 
• Sometimes make the model a bit bigger (but use less data). 
• Sometimes make the data a little bigger (but use fewer params). 
Challenges? 
• Then your final model used only 1/30 of your budget…
15

title: Idea #2: Tune hyperparams at small scale!
text:
Idea #2: Tune hyperparams at small scale!
• Then just copy them over and run them at large scale. 
• Challenge? 
• … turns out they don’t transfer so easily! 
• Best choice at small scale may not be the same at larger scale. 
• As an extreme example, at small scale, sometimes overly strong 
inductive biases might appear to pay off better.
16

title: One approach for finding optimal (N, D)
text:
One approach for finding optimal (N, D)
1.
Pick, say, 4 model sizes: 100M, 300M, 1B, 3B. 
2.
Per size, launch training runs with different LR decay schedules (for, say, D = 20B, 60B, 
180B tokens). Record <compute FLOPs, possibly training loss> throughout training. 
3.
Plot these values and find the lowest achievable loss at any compute C. 
4.
Fit univariate power law for “optimal N vs. C” and/or “optimal D vs. C”. 
5.
Extrapolate both to get optimal (N, D) for a given C. (Or use D ~= C/6N.)

title: Takeaways of Kaplan et al.
text:
Takeaways of Kaplan et al.
• test loss scales as power law of data, parameter count, and compute 
• test loss is more sensitive to parameter count than data: larger compute 
-> increase model by a larger factor than dataset size (later disputed!) 
• larger models require less data to reach same performance, so don’t train 
to convergence — instead: train larger models for fewer steps
This popularized a very different and new way of thinking. 
Is model (# of parameters) scale pretty much all you need?? 
(No, but it was a very useful illusion in some sense!)
26

title: Scaling Laws caveats… Kaplan’20 vs. Chinchilla’22
text:
Scaling Laws caveats… Kaplan’20 vs. Chinchilla’22
DeepMind confirmed the power-law scaling but disputed the optimal 
allocation between data and parameters. Scale them equally! (sqrt of compute) 
Details: They fixed some hyperparameter decisions (data-dependent learning rate schedule) and 
experimented with much larger models (up to 16B in scale). They also counted parameters a little 
differently (embedding parameters counted). 
“Fixed training budget” vs. deployment. 
There’s a shift towards overtraining!

title: Intuition: Let’s break training into stages!
text:
Intuition: Let’s break training into stages!
• Start by pre-training on as much data as possible, even if the 
quality is not perfect. 
• Progressively switch to training on more carefully curated (and 
hence far smaller) datasets. 
• Models learns language and build very strong priors about the 
world in earlier stages. 
• Then use these as learning biases (for generalization!) in later 
stages that teach them the behavior we actually want.

title: Fundamental challenges with SFT…
text:
Fundamental challenges with SFT…
• Is there an objective, single right answer (demonstration) to teach? 
• What if there are many OK answers? 
• What if the model’s answer is even better than our human label? 
• Can the model actually learn the underlying process, which is 
required for generalization, from a bunch of demonstrations?
40

title: Instead of defining a “right answer” for each prompt…
text:
Instead of defining a “right answer” for each prompt…
• What if we define a function R(x, y) that takes the prompt x and our 
model’s own response y and returns a “goodness” score? 
• Q1: How do we define R(x, y)? What do we want to maximize? 
• Q2: How do we maximize the expected reward? 
• Q3: How do we preserve generalization, even if our R(x, y) or our 
distribution of prompts is a little off?
41

Maybe put humans in the training loop? Each step, ask the model to

title: Idea: RL from “Verifiable” Rewards (RLVR)
text:
Idea: RL from “Verifiable” Rewards (RLVR)
• Mainstream models focused on scaling RLHF for a few years. 
It works but doesn’t maximize technical capabilities very rapidly… 
• A simpler view is “supervised RL”. 
• Label answers (or other per-question rubrics). 
• Implement R(x, y) as a high-precision function, not a noisy reward 
model from (rather weak!) human or AI feedback. 
• Not particularly hard or new at all. But only scaled up in late 2024!

Training explicit “reasoning” models that verbalize their chain of thought BEFORE

title: Simplest algorithm: Rejection Fine-Tuning (RFT)
text:
Simplest algorithm: Rejection Fine-Tuning (RFT) 
(aka filtered behavior cloning or guess-and-check; many other names)
• With your current model, for each prompt x, sample K responses. 
• Score each with R(x, y_i). Keep only responses with high reward. 
• Run an “offline” SFT job on the resulting <x, y> pairs. 
• Improvement: Online RFT. For a batch of prompts, sample rollouts 
and take an SFT gradient step to update the model. 
• This can actually take you rather far for many tasks…
49

title: Why might this be insufficient?
text:
Why might this be insufficient?
1. We don’t learn anything from failed examples! 
2. We may memorize sub-optimal answers from early in training and 
fail to progress any further. 
3. We may diverge too far from the original model in a way that 
hinders generalization to *other* distributions of tasks.
50

title: Policy Gradient Algorithms (REINFORCE)
text:
Policy Gradient Algorithms (REINFORCE)
51
• We want to maximize the expected reward, J(θ). How? 
• Thanks to the policy gradient theorem, we can estimate the gradient on 
the left-hand side by just… 
• sampling rollouts y for inputs x and… 
• calculating the gradient of the log-probability of y, 
• weighted by the observed rewards.

title: • Simple & Complicated: Good ideas are often simple! But may only shine
text:
• Simple & Complicated: Good ideas are often simple! But may only shine 
when scaled. This takes a lot of engineering and attention to detail. 
• No Free Lunch: We need biases about our world for ML methods to 
generalize. How should we design such, potentially extensive, biases? 
• Data is Key: We build a general architecture, i.e. the Transformer, and 
train it on the world’s knowledge so it encodes structure from data. 
• Iterating is the Way: We tweak our models until they tend to generalize, 
then curate RL tasks so the model itself also learns from trial and error. 
Is this the right approach? TBD. But the resulting models are outstandingly 
powerful and also quite unreliable and full of unpredictable flaws.
